The '''Thames Rowing Club''' ('''Thames RC''', '''TRC''' or, informally within the rowing community, '''Thames''') is a [[rowing club]] based on the tidal [[River Thames|Thames]] as it flows through the western suburbs of London. The TRC clubhouse stands on [[Putney]] Embankment.<ref>{{cite web
| url=https://www.thamesrc.co.uk/find-us
| title=Find Us
| publisher=Thames Rowing Club
| access-date=8 July 2022
}}</ref> The club was founded in 1860.<ref name="Minute Book 1861-1872">{{cite web |title=Minute Book 1861–1872 |url=https://thamesrcarchive.co.uk/uploads/r/thames-rowing-club-archive/7/0/3/7037d8de114513bbb1a656d3078be73665c636d3e6203e502b71cbc0858a725e/TRC-GOV-2-1_Minute_Book_1861-1872_150dpi.pdf |website=Thames Rowing Club Archive |date=1861–1872 |publisher=Thames Rowing Club |access-date=9 July 2022 |ref=GB TRCA TRC-GOV-2-1}}</ref>{{rp|page=6|style=ama}}

As of July 2025, Thames had won events at [[Henley Royal Regatta]] 94 times.

Thames is one of the founding clubs of [[Remenham Club]]; a social club for rowers, with a clubhouse and grounds on the [[Henley Royal Regatta]] course.<ref>{{cite web
| url=https://www.remenhamclub.co.uk/the-club#CLUBHISTORY
| title=History
| publisher=Remenham Club
| access-date=27 June 2022
}}</ref> Thames hosts [[Cambridge University Women's Boat Club]] for their winter Tideway training ahead of the [[Women's Boat Race]], and on race day itself.<ref>{{cite web
| url=https://cubc.org.uk/news/news/the-womens-eights-head-of-the-river-race/
| title=The Women's Eights Head of the River Race 2020
| date=6 March 2020
| publisher=Cambridge University Boat Club
| access-date=27 June 2022
}}</ref> Thames also houses the [[Boat Race]]'s media centre and administrative office.

The club colours are red, white and black in stripes, the white stripe lying between the red and black and being of half their width.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.thamesrc.co.uk/site/about_thames/rules_and_byelaws.php |title=Rules and byelaws |access-date=2011-05-29 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110719143801/http://www.thamesrc.co.uk/site/about_thames/rules_and_byelaws.php |archive-date=19 July 2011 }}</ref>

==History==
===Foundation===
Thames Rowing Club was founded under the name [[City of London]] Rowing Club and according to its first rules, its objects were 'organised pleasure or exercise rowing'.<ref name=Page>{{cite book
  | author= Page, Geoffrey
  | author-link= Geoffrey Page (rower)
  | title = Hear The Boat Sing: the history of Thames Rowing Club and tideway rowing
  | publisher = Kingswood Press
  | date = 1991
  | isbn = 0-413-65410-9}}</ref>{{rp|page=3|style=ama}} The earliest surviving minutes of a club meeting are dated January 1861 but are headed 'City of London Rowing Club. Established 1860', and 1860 is commonly accepted as the year of foundation.<ref name= "Minute Book 1861-1872"/>{{rp|page=6|style=ama}}

The initial members were chiefly clerks and salesmen working in London's textiles trade around Fore Street and St Paul's Churchyard.<ref>{{cite book
  | last1=Lehmann
  | first1=Rudolf Chambers
  | author-link1=R. C. Lehmann
  | contributor-last1=Eyre
  | contributor-first1=William Henry
  | contribution=The Thames Rowing Club: their methods of training and their victories from 1874–1882
  | title = The Complete Oarsman
  | publisher = Methuen
  | orig-date = First published 1908
  | date = 1931
  | edition = 4th
  | page = 179
  | oclc = 6540426}}</ref> The early meetings are known to have taken place in the Lord Raglan [[public house]] in [[St Martin's-le-Grand]].<ref name= "Minute Book 1861-1872"/>{{rp|page=12|style=ama}} The club had boats at Simmons Boathouse (the building currently occupied by Chas Newens Marine) and a room at the Red Lion Hotel at the foot of Putney High Street.<ref name=Page/>{{rp|page=3|style=ama}} There were very few members at first, but the numbers rapidly increased, and in 1862, when club races were first started, the club numbered nearly 150.

In 1862, the club sought and gained the permission of [[Francis Playford|Frank Playford]], the only traceable member of "The Thames Club" which had rowed on the [[Tideway]] in the 1840s, to rename itself "The Thames Rowing Club".<ref name=Page/>{{rp|page=4|style=ama}}

===Early successes===
By 1864 a growing interest in competition led to the club's first recorded win, in a four-oared race against the Excelsior Boat Club of Greenwich. The club also put on a crew for the Metropolitan Junior Eights, started in 1865, and followed this up the next year by securing the Challenge Cup for Junior Eights at the first [[Metropolitan Regatta]].<ref name=Page/>{{rp|page=4|style=ama}}

In 1870 the Club won at [[Henley Royal Regatta]] for the first time, taking the [[Wyfold Challenge Cup]] from the Oscillators Club of Surbiton and the Oxford Etonians in a race that, according to the Rowing Almanack, was ‘a pretty hollow affair, the Thames crew winning as they pleased from first to last.’<ref name=Page/>{{rp|page=8|style=ama}}

Over the next twenty years, Thames had its first great flowering, with 22 wins at Henley by 1890, including four victories in the most prestigious event, the [[Grand Challenge Cup]] for eights.<ref name= "Steward 1903" >
{{cite book
  | last1=Steward
  | first1=Herbert Thomas
  | title = The Records of Henley Royal Regatta from its institution in 1839 to 1902
  | publisher = Grant Richards
  | publication-place = London
  | date = 1903
  | oclc = 58443538}}
</ref>

In 1877 the Thames Boathouse Company (Limited) was formed for the purpose of providing a boat and club house for the club. Money was raised by means of shares, the club and the company being kept quite distinct.<ref name="Minute Book 1872-1880">{{cite web |title=Minute Book 1872–1880 |url=https://thamesrcarchive.co.uk/uploads/r/thames-rowing-club-archive/9/0/d/90dddf97fdfc92ffd0912ab8dd8123475228e7fe843dcf0f93291493980fca63/TRC-GOV-2-2_Committee_Minutes_1872-1880_150dpi.pdf |website=Thames Rowing Club Archive |publisher=Thames Rowing Club |access-date=9 July 2022 |date=1872–1880|ref=GB TRCA TRC-GOV-2-2}}</ref>{{rp|pages=51–52|style=ama}} The construction of the present Thames boathouse on a site about 300 yards above that of [[London Rowing Club]] followed and the building was completed in 1879 at a cost of over £3000.<ref name="Dickens 1887">{{cite book |editor1-last=Dickens
|editor1-first=Charles
|editor-link1=Charles Dickens Jr.
|title=Dickens's Dictionary of the Thames 1887 |date=1994 |publisher=Old House Books |isbn=1873590121 |edition=2nd}}</ref>{{rp|page=245|style=ama}}

Thames, under its captain [[James Hastie (rower)|James Hastie]], was now established as a mainstay of amateur rowing in London, and as a rival to its Putney neighbour [[London Rowing Club]].<ref>{{cite book
 |editor1-last=Page
 |editor1-first=William
 |title=A History of the County of Middlesex
 |date=1911
 |volume=2 General; Ashford, East Bedfont With Hatton, Feltham, Hampton With Hampton Wick, Hanworth, Laleham, Littleton
 |publisher=Victoria County History
 |location=London
 |pages=283–292
 |url=https://www.british-history.ac.uk/vch/middx/vol2/pp283-292
 |access-date=9 July 2022
|chapter=Sport, ancient and modern: Pastimes
 |via=British History Online}}</ref> In 1879 Thames, like London, was one of the founder clubs of the Metropolitan Rowing Association which later became the [[British Rowing|Amateur Rowing Association (ARA)]].<ref>
{{cite book
  | last1=Woodgate
  | first1=Walter Bradford
  | author-link1=Walter Bradford Woodgate
  | series=The Badminton Library of Sports and Pastimes
  | title = Boating
  | publisher = Longmans, Green, & Co.
  | date = 1888
  | page = 195
  | oclc = 3859855
}}
</ref> As a result, Thames was one of five clubs which had the right until 2012 to appoint representatives to the Council of the ARA and its successor [[British Rowing]].  The others were [[Leander Club]], [[London Rowing Club]], [[Oxford University Boat Club]] and [[Cambridge University Boat Club]].<ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.britishrowing.org/about-us/strategy-structure | title=Corporate Governance Structure | publisher=British Rowing | access-date=31 January 2013 | url-status=dead | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130120001107/http://www.britishrowing.org/about-us/strategy-structure | archive-date=20 January 2013}}</ref>

This early period was the time of the great Victorian amateur.  Many Thames members were keen on all sports and the club itself also had an influence beyond rowing:

In December 1867, Thames organised a two and a half mile handicap steeplechase or paperchase similar to a [[cross country running|cross-country]] race around [[Wimbledon Common]] as part of the oarsmen's winter training.  These are generally accepted as the first open cross-country events to have taken place in Britain.  One eventual result was the foundation of the [[Thames Hare and Hounds]] in October 1868, the first cross-country club, which would itself go on to an illustrious history.<ref>
{{cite book
  | last1=Ryan
  | first1=James
  | last2=Fraser
  | first2=Ian H.
  | title = The annals of Thames Hare and Hounds 1868–1945
  | publisher = Thames Hare and Hounds
  | date = 1968
  | oclc = 877578362
  | isbn = 9780901132000}}
</ref>

Another addition to rowing training was boxing, with a ring frequently set up in the hall at the clubhouse.  George Vize, a member of five winning crews at Henley, became amateur heavyweight champion of Britain in 1878 and a founder member of the [[Amateur Boxing Association of England|Amateur Boxing Association]].  Boxing finally disappeared after the First World War, when the coach [[Steve Fairbairn]] ended it because of the damage caused to oarsmen's hands.<ref name=Page/>{{rp|page=10|style=ama}}

===From the 20th Century to the present day===
From the late 1890s into the first decade of the 20th century, Thames suffered a decline but recovered as the decade wore on, notably through the efforts of [[Julius Beresford]] and [[Karl Vernon]].<ref name=Page/>{{rp|pages=45–53|style=ama}}

After the [[First World War]], Thames came under the influence of the coach Steve Fairbairn.  Fairbairn was an Australian graduate of Cambridge, with boundless charisma and innovative (and highly controversial) views on training and technique.  He was one of the major influences on the club and on the sport in general, becoming generally accepted as the father of modern rowing.  Under his tutelage in the 1920s, and that of [[Julius Beresford]], Thames reached new heights.  Fairbairn left the club for [[London Rowing Club]] in 1925. The precise reasons are unclear but undoubtedly a clash with Julius Beresford was partly at the root: the two coaches, despite holding similar views on technique, were unable to get on. Under Beresford, Thames won four events at Henley in both 1927 and 1928, something which no club replicated in the 20th century.<ref name=Page/><ref name= "Steward 1939" >
{{cite book
  | last1=Steward
  | first1=Clifford Thomas
  | title = Henley Records 1919–1938
  | publisher = Hamish Hamilton
  | publication-place = London
  | date = 1939
  | oclc = 29252608}}
</ref>{{rp|pages=167–208|style=ama}}

At the same time, Thames was home to Britain's greatest ever single sculler.  [[Jack Beresford]] (son of Julius) took Silver at the 1920 Amsterdam Olympics in an epic race with [[John B. Kelly Sr.|Jack Kelly]], before going one better with Gold at Paris in 1924.  He won the [[Diamond Challenge Sculls|Diamond Sculls]] at Henley four times and the [[Wingfield Sculls]] for the Amateur championship of Great Britain a record seven times. Then, with Thames crews, he took three further Olympic medals: Silver in the eight in Antwerp, 1928, Gold in the coxless four in Los Angeles, 1932 and Gold in the double scull in Berlin, 1936.  It would be 60 years before [[Steve Redgrave]] bettered his record.<ref name=Page/>{{rp|pages=57–94|style=ama}}

Although never again reaching the heights of the late 1920s, Thames continued to be successful through the thirties and then, after the [[Second World War]], into the forties and fifties.  However, in the early sixties the club began to experience a marked decline in membership and standards. By the early seventies Thames had very few active members and came close to bankruptcy.  The club went for 47 years from 1956 without a win by a men's crew at [[Henley Royal Regatta]].<ref name=Page/>{{rp|pages=97–141|style=ama}}

In 1972, Thames became one of the first British rowing clubs to admit women and rapidly became the powerhouse of women's rowing, a position it retains to this day.<ref name=Page/>{{rp|page=143|style=ama}} Thames women represented Great Britain at every Olympic Games between [[1984 Summer Olympics|Los Angeles]] and [[2008 Summer Olympics|Beijing]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Thames Rowing Club, Putney (GBR) |url=http://www.olympedia.org/affiliations/917 |website=Olympedia |publisher=OlyMADMen |access-date=10 July 2022}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Elise Laverick |url=http://www.olympedia.org/athletes/92562 |website=Olympedia |publisher=OlyMADMen |access-date=10 July 2022}}</ref> Sisters [[Guin Batten]] and [[Miriam Batten]] won Silver in the quadruple scull at the [[2000 Summer Olympics|Sydney Olympics]].<ref>{{cite web |title=SYDNEY 2000 ROWING QUADRUPLE SCULLS WITHOUT COXSW WOMEN RESULTS |url=https://olympics.com/en/olympic-games/sydney-2000/results/rowing/quadruple-sculls-without-coxsw-women |website=Olympics.com |publisher=International Olympic Committee |access-date=10 July 2022}}</ref> [[Elise Laverick]] won Bronze in the double scull at the [[2004 Summer Olympics|Athens Olympics]] in 2004<ref>{{cite web |title=ATHENS 2004 ROWING DOUBLE SCULLS 2X WOMEN RESULTS |url=https://olympics.com/en/olympic-games/athens-2004/results/rowing/double-sculls-2x-women |website=Olympics.com |publisher=International Olympic Committee |access-date=10 July 2022}}</ref> and in the [[2008 Summer Olympics|Beijing Olympics]] in 2008.<ref>{{cite web |title=BEIJING 2008 ROWING DOUBLE SCULLS 2X WOMEN RESULTS |url=https://olympics.com/en/olympic-games/beijing-2008/results/rowing/double-sculls-2x-women |website=Olympics.com |publisher=International Olympic Committee |access-date=10 July 2022}}</ref> Since the founding of [[Henley Women's Regatta]] in 1987, the club has won there 55 times with the most recent wins being the aspirational club eights in 2022.<ref>
{{cite web
| url=https://hwr.org.uk/results-archive/
| title=Results from All Years
| publisher=Henley Women's Regatta
| access-date=24 June 2022
}}
</ref>

In 2003, Thames achieved an emphatic win in the [[Wyfold Challenge Cup]] ending 47 years without a men's win at Henley.<ref>
{{cite web
| url=https://thamesrcarchive.co.uk/index.php/image-13
| title=Wyfold winning crew 2003
| publisher=Thames Rowing Club Archive
| access-date=24 June 2022
}}
</ref>

In 2005, Thames crews reached the finals of the [[Wyfold Challenge Cup]], the [[Britannia Challenge Cup]], the [[Princess Grace Challenge Cup]] (for women's quadruple sculls) and the [[Remenham Challenge Cup]] (for women's eights). The club won the last of these – the first win by a solely Thames women's crew at Henley Royal Regatta.<ref>
{{cite web
| url=https://thamesrcarchive.co.uk/index.php/image-15
| title=The winning Remenham Cup VIII
| publisher=Thames Rowing Club Archive
| access-date=24 June 2022
}}
</ref>

In 2006 came another win in the [[Wyfold Challenge Cup]].<ref>
{{cite web
| url=https://thamesrcarchive.co.uk/index.php/image-03
| title=Wyfold winning crew 2006
| publisher=Thames Rowing Club Archive
| access-date=24 June 2022
}}
</ref>

There then followed a period where, despite coming close, there were no Henley wins. However, in 2015 Thames won the [[Thames Challenge Cup]] for club eights, the first time the club had done so since 1934.<ref>{{cite web
| url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_O8XC2PzF1A
| title=Leverkusen v Thames Finals Day Henley 2015 Thames
| date=5 July 2015
| publisher=HenleyRoyalRegatta
| access-date=24 June 2022
}}
</ref>
This was followed in 2016 by a win in the [[Visitors' Challenge Cup]] for intermediate coxless fours – the first win for Thames in this event.<ref>
{{cite web
| url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aaZoK_MxbOQ
| title=Visitors' Final – Thames v California Berkeley Henley 2016
| date=3 July 2016
| publisher=HenleyRoyalRegatta
| access-date=24 June 2022
}}
</ref>

In 2017, there was an unprecedented achievement: two Thames crews reached the final of the [[Thames Challenge Cup]], with Thames A beating Thames B by 5 lengths.<ref>
{{cite web
| url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NGBawBqqwq4
| title=Thames Final – Thames 'B' v Thames 'A' Henley 2017
| date=2 July 2017
| publisher=HenleyRoyalRegatta
| access-date=24 June 2022
}}
</ref>

The following year, Thames retained the [[Thames Challenge Cup]], and won the [[Britannia Challenge Cup]] for the first time in its history, setting a course record in the process.<ref>
{{cite web
| url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6Ydvs0UvoK0
| title=Thames Final – Thames 'A' v Oslo, NOR Henley 2018
| date=8 July 2018
| publisher=HenleyRoyalRegatta
| access-date=24 June 2022
}}
</ref><ref>
{{cite web
| url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SmeKjdYHQkw
| title=Brittannia Final – Molesey 'A' v Thames 'A' Henley 2018
| date=8 July 2018
| publisher=HenleyRoyalRegatta
| access-date=24 June 2022
}}</ref>

There were no wins in 2019, and in 2020 the regatta did not take place owing to the [[COVID-19 pandemic]].<ref name=cov>{{cite web|url=https://www.hrr.co.uk/2020-regatta-cancellation-statement-coronavirus-covid-19|title=2020 REGATTA CANCELLATION – STATEMENT ON CORONAVIRUS (COVID-19)|website=Henley Royal Regatta |date=14 July 2025 }}</ref>

In 2021, Thames reached four Henley finals for the first time since 2005: the [[Thames Challenge Cup]], the [[Wyfold Challenge Cup]], the [[Princess Grace Challenge Cup]] and the new [[Wargrave Challenge Cup]] for club women's eights, going on to win the Thames and the Wyfold (the latter for the first time since 2006).<ref>
{{cite web
| url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_dgZgD4yssU
| title=Thames Final – Molesey BC A v Thames RC A Henley 2021
| date=15 August 2021
| publisher=Henley Royal Regatta
| access-date=4 July 2022
}}
</ref><ref>
{{cite web
| url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_UVLlhZ0emM
| title=Wyfold Final – Lea RC v Thames RC A, Henley 2021
| date=15 August 2021
| publisher=Henley Royal Regatta
| access-date=4 July 2022
}}
</ref>

At the 2022 regatta, Thames again reached four finals – this time of the [[Wargrave Challenge Cup]], [[Thames Challenge Cup]], [[Wyfold Challenge Cup]] and [[Britannia Challenge Cup]]. There were wins in all but the Thames, to give the club its most successful Henley Royal Regatta since 1928.<ref>
{{cite web
| url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tGYLLek4Gnk
| title=Wyfold Final – Thames R.C. v N.S.R. Oslo, Henley 2022
| date=3 July 2022
| publisher=Henley Royal Regatta
| access-date=4 July 2022
}}
</ref><ref>
{{cite web
| url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Kq-YJNujZxk
| title=Britannia Final – London RC 'A' v Thames RC, Henley 2022
| date=3 July 2022
| publisher=Henley Royal Regatta
| access-date=4 July 2022
}}
</ref><ref>
{{cite web
| url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5bO-dmsmZQM
| title=Wargrave Final – Thames RC. 'A' v Leander Club, Henley 2022
| date=3 July 2022
| publisher=Henley Royal Regatta
| access-date=4 July 2022
}}
</ref> In the final of the Wargrave, the Thames crew set new records to all of the timing markers.<ref>{{cite web |title=Henley Sunday: Morning Mass
 |last=Koch
 |first=Tim
 |url=https://heartheboatsing.com/2022/07/07/henley-sunday-morning-mass/ |website=Hear The Boat Sing |date=7 July 2022
 |access-date=9 July 2022}}</ref>

Rowing by older oarsmen (and more recently oarswomen) has been a part of the club's activities throughout its history, but has increased since the 1970s in line with more national and FISA (international) Masters Competition now on offer.  A group of casual and veteran men came into existence in the 1970s; separate groups of masters oarsmen and women of different ages have since arisen from time to time.

==Clubhouse==
[[File:Thames Rowing Club, Putney Embankment (geograph 2106050).jpg|thumb|Clubhouse before 2011 renovations]]
The clubhouse itself was constructed in 1879 with several later additions.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://thamesrc.co.uk/site/clubhouse/index.php |title=The TRC Clubhouse |access-date=2011-05-29 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110830175537/http://thamesrc.co.uk/site/clubhouse/index.php |archive-date=30 August 2011 }}</ref> In 2005, the club opened a new building behind the clubhouse, named in memory of former club President and benefactor [[Alan Burrough]], providing additional training facilities and boat storage.<ref>{{cite web |title=Item 00683 – Opening of the Burrough Building |url=https://www.thamesrcarchive.co.uk/index.php/trc-pho-1-00683 |website=Thames Rowing Club Archive |publisher=Thames Rowing Club |access-date=10 July 2022 |ref=GB TRCA TRC-PHO-1-00683 |date=15 May 2005}}</ref> In May 2011, work began on substantial alterations and improvements to the clubhouse.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.thamesrc.co.uk/site/news/archive/clubhouse_building_works_start.php |title= Clubhouse building works start |access-date=2011-05-29 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110719143233/http://www.thamesrc.co.uk/site/news/archive/clubhouse_building_works_start.php |archive-date=19 July 2011 }}</ref> The clubhouse is an approved venue for wedding and civil partnership ceremonies.<ref>{{cite web |title=Approved ceremony venues – Thames Rowing Club |url=https://wandsworth.gov.uk/births-death-and-ceremonies/ceremony-venues/approved-ceremony-venues/thames-rowing-club/ |website=wandsworth.gov.uk |publisher=Wandsworth Council |access-date=13 July 2022}}</ref>
